Since April 2025, center- or far-right forces have won power in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Honduras, and Peru. In Argentina, President Javier Milei’s populist party secured a decisive victory in midterm elections last October. NEW YORK—It is telling that Anthropic chose to call its most powerful AI model “Mythos.” In ancient Greek, the word denotes an original reality that we can imitate or embody through the stories we tell ourselves and one another. Pliny the Elder tells us that the fifth-century Greek painter Zeuxis rendered grapes so realistically as to fool even the birds.

PARIS—Given current AI capabilities, does it matter who conducts scientific research? The intuitive response is that a fact is a fact, regardless of who finds it. But knowledge is never disseminated that way. We receive most scientific claims without any means of checking them ourselves, so we tend to judge not the claim but the credibility of whoever stands behind it. As the Harvard historian of science Steven Shapinshows, the production of scientific truth has long been inseparable from the social work of persuading one’s peers.

Brazil’s right-wing presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, is promising an economic policy that would follow Milei’s lead, and US President Donald Trump calls him his “favorite president.” Last year, Trump extended Argentina an unprecedented $20 billion currency swap line to halt its currency’s free fall on the eve of legislative elections, and the gambit worked. PARIS—Hundreds of thousands of young people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the state of the country’s education system. The violence that erupted on October 17 should not eclipse their concerns, which are entirely legitimate: the deplorable conditions at many French schools, including dilapidated buildings, a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days. They are also deeply opposed to Parcoursup, the country’s university-admissions platform, which has become the lightning rod for their grievances. They have denounced it as opaque, stressful, and unfair.

When the main demonstration assembled at 2 p.m. at the Place de la République, we were hiking in the forests southeast of Paris near Fontainebleau, once an autumnal retreat and hunting ground for French kings.

WASHINGTON, DC—The International Labour Organization (ILO) was established at a time when, much like today, society was riven by vast inequalities. In the years before World War I, workers’ militant organizing and mass strikes alarmed employers and governments. The premise of the ILO Constitution, adopted in 1919, was that collective bargaining could prevent revolution by turning class conflict into negotiated, shared gains.

This arrangement assumed that an international floor for labor standards would halt a race to the bottom on wages and working conditions as countries compete for trade and investment. For roughly three decades after World War II, that assumption generally held up, benefiting millions of workers, though mostly in formal employment in the industrialized Global North.

It is no longer the case today. The UN’s 2026 Sustainable Development Goals Annual Report notes that the weakening of labor rights worldwide is “leaving many increasingly constrained or unable to organize or bargain collectively.” According to the International Trade Union Confederation’s Global Rights Index, 80% of the 121 countries surveyed restricted collective bargaining in 2026, and 87% restricted the right to strike. The OECD also reports that union density has been falling in its member economies for decades. In many countries, capital is more concentrated, and governments are more captured by it, than at any time in the last century.

The unraveling of the 1919 compromise was not an accident. The relationship between firm and worker, and the corresponding obligations, were intentionally severed through vertical disintegration across global supply chains, subcontracting, and labor intermediation. Digital-platform work, the most recent manifestation of this, relies on widespread employment misclassification that denies millions of workers their legal rights.

Although global value chains have been a reality of manufacturing and services for decades, not enough progress has been made on negotiating global rules to protect workers’ rights and hold lead firms accountable. Employers’ opposition to standard-setting on this issue at the ILO remains deeply entrenched. They insist that, instead of regulating their practices, we should focus on getting results from labor inspectorates—government agencies that are usually underfunded and disempowered—at the site of manufacture or service provision.

Many countries no longer have the capacity or the incentive to legislate a global rights floor, owing to economic liberalization and capital mobility. At the same time, investors have acquired and used provisions of trade and investment agreements to sue governments directly over laws and policies that might affect their profitability. Moreover, governments put other priorities ahead of enforcing laws that would help raise living standards. Even the novel “rapid response labor mechanism” under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, designed to promote freedom of association and collective bargaining at the firm level, is faltering for lack of political will.

Addressing these problems will require more than another declaration. Organized workers and the fear of revolution produced the bargain of 1919. The ILO Constitution merely ratified what worker power had already achieved. Its premise remains valid—and a robust global labor architecture is still necessary—but the assumption that compromise was somehow self-executing was always mistaken. Instead, workers’ organizations have been steadily undermined by regressive legislation and a multi-billion-dollar industry that supports employers’ “union avoidance” efforts.

Fulfilling the ILO’s promise requires a concerted global effort to create an enabling environment for all workers and their organizations to organize and bargain collectively, at home, across borders, and down supply chains, where decision-makers are located. Countervailing power must be rebuilt, including by ensuring that labor can operate across borders as easily as capital does. That means institutionalizing transnational collective bargaining, as well as sectoral bargaining and extension mechanisms (which spread union contracts to other workers). Solidarity action needs to be protected, or else the right to strike can do little good when decision-makers are located elsewhere. And vulnerable workers—including the two billion informal workers, digital-platform workers, and dependent self-employed workers—require an effective right to organize and bargain.

Labor rights must be an effective feature of international economic governance as well. While the ILO supervisory system may have persuasive remedies, they need legal regimes to give them effect. Compliance will never be mandated in Geneva. It must be enforced through constitutional litigation, regional human-rights courts, trade agreements, and procurement and financial regulations. That could mean rapid, trade-linked remedies against companies that violate workers’ fundamental rights, and enforceable supply-chain agreements between workers, brands, and suppliers.

With the world poised to overshoot the Paris climate agreement’s target of limiting global warming to 1.5° Celsius, these reforms have become essential. The climate crisis is also a crisis of workers’ rights, and addressing one can address the other. Global warming is already affecting workers, whether through job displacement in carbon-intensive industries or through extreme heat, crop failure, coastal erosion, and other disasters. While workers and trade unions are widely recognized as indispensable actors in any just climate transition, the legal infrastructure needed to ensure that they have a voice in shaping that transition is underdeveloped or non-existent in many countries.

Finally, the expansion of AI, automated management, and digital surveillance is rapidly transforming work, threatening jobs and fundamental rights, and further exacerbating inequality, from warehouses to digital labor platforms.

Where workers’ organizations once could bargain effectively, now authoritarian oligarchs largely control the levers of power. That need not be the case. We can reverse this lopsided dynamic, but only if workers can lawfully organize and act on the same scale as capital. Addressing the challenges of our time depends on it.

But these issues have since receded from the forefront of our concerns, overshadowed by anxiety over the AI boom and possible bust, rising bond yields, and mounting public debt.

YEREVAN—In times of war, geopolitical turmoil, and fiscal tightening, it is tempting to view the defense of nature as a desirable but non-urgent goal—an objective that can be pursued when calmer times return. But we embrace this view at our peril.

As world leaders gather for the United Nations biodiversity and climate-change conferences this fall, they must remember that over half of global GDP depends on nature and the services it provides. Healthy soils underpin a $9.5 trillion global food industry, while forests support 1.5 billion livelihoods around the world. Healthy rivers help absorb floodwaters and sustain vital transportation networks. Nature is the backbone of the global economy, and protecting it must be a top national and international priority.

Nature-related crises won’t wait until the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are over. This summer’s sweltering drought in Europe caused $2-3 billion in crop losses, a double blow for farmers after the war-induced closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused fertilizer prices to surge by 71%. The combined effects of conflict and extreme weather have helped push global food prices to their highest levels since 2022.

All told, scientists predict that a partial collapse of ecosystems could cost the global economy $2.7 trillion annually. Despite intense geopolitical instability, we cannot afford to undermine the natural systems on which our economies depend. The global goal to protect and conserve at least 30% of the world’s land and ocean by 2030, known as 30x30, is more important than ever.

Protecting nature is an investment in resilience and solidarity. Resilience strengthens food and water security, and the capacity to weather climate shocks. It sustains livelihoods, public health, and long-term economic stability. The 30x30 goal, adopted by governments in 2022 under the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, recognizes that protecting nature is fundamental to providing these and other public goods.

For example, kelp beds, mangroves, and marshes absorb carbon dioxide, while coral reefs help protect against storms and provide natural habitats for some of the world’s most diverse ecosystems. On land, forests regulate rainfall and support the livelihoods of local communities, and healthy soils retain water and nutrients that are vital to global food security and flood protection.

Four years on, the world has made significant strides toward the 30x30 goal. New analysis from Campaign for Nature shows that 20% of land and inland waters are now designated as protected or conserved, and that fully delivering on existing commitments could increase this share to approximately 27% by 2030, closing much of the remaining gap.

Progress at sea, however, has been much slower. Only 10% of the ocean is formally designated for conservation, and existing commitments would increase this to a mere 12% by 2030. Worse, Together for the Ocean’s latest Ocean Protection Gap Report finds that only 3.5% of the ocean is assessed as effectively protected, with harmful activities continuing in many areas that are supposed to be off limits.

With just four years remaining, the world still has a chance to achieve 30x30, which is one of the defining global commitments of this decade. But what will it take to make up for lost time?

For starters, governments must dramatically increase financing for nature. Delivering 30x30 will require approximately $100–180 billion annually, compared with current annual spending of $24 billion. But, again, this spending represents an investment, not just a cost. Achieving 30x30 could add up to $450 billion to annual global GDP by 2050 and support an estimated 4–7 million jobs.

Policymakers at all levels urgently must move from talking about solutions to implementing them. As of May 2026, 116 countries had submitted commitments to protect up to 27% of land and inland water areas. But many have yet to follow up with mapped, costed, and financed plans. Commitments alone will not protect nature.

Protecting more of the planet is only part of the challenge. Governments also must ensure that protected and conserved areas are well managed, deliver real benefits, and meaningfully preserve biodiversity. That requires long-term funding arrangements that can endure through changing economic and political cycles.

There is no denying that the global outlook is uncertain. The wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are spurring governments to increase spending on defense and focus more on economic growth. But it would be a mistake to put nature on the back burner. Protecting natural systems is not just for the bees. Investing in their future is an investment in our own.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: SEOUL—Discussion of economic inequality usually focuses on disparities across countries or the divide between rich and poor households within them. But greater attention is now being devoted to domestic regional differences, whether between the capital city and the rest of the country (as in South Korea and the United Kingdom), between northern and southern regions (as in Italy), or between coastal cities and inland areas (as in China and the United States).
STOCKHOLM—As the term “middle powers” has gained currency this year, it has forced us to ask which countries actually belong to this grouping. After all, shouldn’t most states be described that way?

ATHENS—On a recent visit to Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extolled ancient Greece as the foundation of Western civilization and drew inspiration for the United States today as the leader of the West. Rubio’s speech at the Pnyx, a hill west of the Acropolis where democracy was first practiced, was a bold and eloquent attempt to trace MAGA’s ideological roots back to Athenian democracy, as well as to Christendom, important discoveries, and imperial conquests. And it was about “us” and “them”: the West and the rest.

PRETORIA—The choice of South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for this year’s Nobel Peace Prize was a striking show of support for the rules-based multilateral system. It was also a slap in the face to US President Donald Trump, who has shamelessly lobbied for the prize while simultaneously attacking the international legal order. At a political rally shortly after the announcement, Trump dismissed Pillay as “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of.”

But the system, ostensibly aimed at bringing order to the country’s chaotic roads, quickly generated controversy.

CAMBRIDGE—Information is undergoing a category change. It has always been something people consume, but it is also becoming something machines act on. That means errors will stop being mere digital impressions and start becoming actions with far-reaching consequences. Given the risks, the system will need safeguards of its own. Better data or putting a human back in the loop will not suffice.
